In [[mathematics]], the '''Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem''' is a theorem of [[Riemannian geometry]], according to which the [[Riemannian metric]] is locally determined by the [[Riemann curvature tensor]], or in other words, behavior of the curvature tensor under parallel translation determines the metric.

The theorem is named after [[Élie Cartan]], [[Warren Ambrose]], and his PhD student Noel Hicks.<ref>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=7688 Mathematics Genealogy Project], entry for Noel Justin Hicks</ref> Cartan proved the local version. Ambrose proved a global version that allows for isometries between general [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian manifolds]] with varying curvature, in 1956.<ref name="Ambrose 1956 p=337">{{cite journal|last=Ambrose|first=W.|year=1956|title=Parallel Translation of Riemannian Curvature|journal=The Annals of Mathematics|publisher=JSTOR|volume=64|issue=2|page=337|doi=10.2307/1969978|issn=0003-486X}}</ref> This was further generalized by Hicks to general manifolds with [[Affine connection|affine connections]] in their [[Tangent bundle|tangent bundles]], in 1959.<ref name="Library 2009 pp. 242–254">{{cite journal|last=Hicks|first=Noel|date=1959|title=A theorem on affine connexions|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ijm/1255455125|journal=Illinois Journal of Mathematics|volume=3|issue=2|pages=242–254|doi=10.1215/ijm/1255455125|issn=0019-2082|doi-access=free}}</ref>

A statement and proof of the theorem can be found in <ref name="Cheeger 2008 p.">{{cite book|title=Comparison theorems in Riemannian geometry|last=Cheeger|first=Jeff|last2=Ebin|first2=David G.|publisher=AMS Chelsea Pub|year=2008|isbn=0-8218-4417-2|publication-place=Providence, R.I|chapter=Chapter 1, Section 12, The Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks Theorem|oclc=185095562}}</ref>

== Introduction ==

Let <math>M,N</math> be connected, complete Riemannian manifolds. We consider the problem of isometrically mapping a small patch on <math>M</math> to a small patch on <math>N</math>.

Let <math>x\in M,y\in N</math>, and let

: <math>I:T_xM\rightarrow T_yN</math>

be a linear [[isometry]]. This can be interpreted as isometrically mapping an [[infinitesimal]] patch (the [[tangent space]]) at <math>x</math> to an infinitesimal patch at <math>y</math>. Now we attempt to extend it to a finite (rather than infinitesimal) patch.

For sufficiently small <math>r>0</math>, the [[Exponential map (Riemannian geometry)|exponential maps]]

: <math>\exp_x:B_r(x)\subset T_xM\rightarrow M, \exp_y:B_r(y)\subset T_yN\rightarrow N</math>

are local diffeomorphisms. Here, <math>B_r(x)</math> is the ball centered on <math>x</math> of radius <math>r.</math> One then defines a diffeomorphism <math>f:B_r(x)\rightarrow B_r(y)</math> by

: <math>f=\exp_y\circ I\circ \exp_x^{-1}.</math>
When is <math>f</math> an isometry? Intuitively, it should be an isometry if it satisfies the two conditions:

* It is a linear isometry at the tangent space of every point on <math>B_r(x)</math>, that is, it is an isometry on the infinitesimal patches.
* It preserves the [[Riemann curvature tensor|curvature tensor]] at the tangent space of every point on <math>B_r(x)</math>, that is, it preserves how the infinitesimal patches fit together.

If <math>f</math> is an isometry, it must preserve the geodesics. Thus, it is natural to consider the behavior of <math>f</math> as we transport it along an arbitrary [[geodesic]] radius <math>\gamma:\left[0,T\right]\rightarrow B_r(x)\subset M</math> starting at <math>\gamma(0)=x</math>. By property of the exponential mapping, <math>f</math> maps it to a geodesic radius of <math>B_r(y)</math> starting at <math>f(\gamma)(0)=y</math>,. 

Let <math>P_\gamma(t)</math> be the [[parallel transport]] along <math>\gamma</math> (defined by the [[Levi-Civita connection]]), and <math>P_{f(\gamma)(t)}</math> be the parallel transport along <math>f(\gamma)</math>, then we have the mapping between infinitesimal patches along the two geodesic radii:

: <math>I_\gamma(t)=P_{f(\gamma)(t)}\circ I\circ P_{\gamma(t)}^{-1}:T_{\gamma(t)}M\rightarrow T_{f(\gamma(t))}N \quad \text{ for all } t\in [0, T]</math>

== Cartan's theorem ==

The original theorem proven by [[Élie Cartan|Cartan]] is the local version of the Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem. <blockquote><math>f</math> is an isometry if and only if for all geodesic radii <math>\gamma:\left[0,T\right]\rightarrow B_r(x)\subset M</math> with <math>\gamma(0)=x</math>, and all <math>t\in [0, T], X,Y,Z\in T_{\gamma(t)}M</math>,  we have <math>I_{\gamma}(t)(R(X,Y,Z))=\overline{R}(I_{\gamma}(t)(X), I_\gamma(t)(Y), I_{\gamma}(t)(Z))</math>

where <math>R,\overline{R}</math> are Riemann curvature tensors of <math>M,N</math>.</blockquote>In words, it states that <math>f</math> is an isometry if and only if the only way to preserve its infinitesimal isometry also preserves the Riemannian curvature.

Note that <math>f</math> generally does not have to be a [[diffeomorphism]], but only a locally isometric [[covering map]]. However, <math>f</math> must be a global isometry if <math>N</math> is simply connected.

== Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem ==

'''Theorem''': For Riemann curvature tensors <math>R,\overline{R}</math> and all broken geodesics (a broken geodesic is a curve that is piecewise geodesic) <math>\gamma:\left[0,T\right]\rightarrow M</math> with <math>\gamma(0)=x</math>, suppose that

: <math>I_\gamma(t)(R(X,Y,Z))=\overline{R}(I_\gamma(t)(X), I_\gamma(t)(Y), I_\gamma(t)(Z))</math>

for all <math>t\in [0, T], X,Y,Z\in T_{\gamma(t)}M</math>.

Then, if two broken geodesics beginning at <math>x</math> have the same endpoint, the corresponding broken geodesics (mapped by <math>I_\gamma</math>) in <math>N</math> also have the same end point. Consequently, there exists a map <math>F:M\rightarrow N</math> defined
by mapping the broken geodesic endpoints in <math>M</math> to the corresponding geodesic endpoints in <math>N</math>.

The map <math>F:M\rightarrow N</math> is a locally isometric covering map.

If <math>N</math> is also simply connected, then <math>F</math> is an isometry.

== Locally symmetric spaces ==

A Riemannian manifold is called ''locally symmetric'' if its Riemann curvature tensor is invariant under parallel transport:

: <math>\nabla R=0.</math>

A simply connected Riemannian manifold is locally symmetric if it is a [[symmetric space]].

From the Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem, we have:

'''Theorem''': Let <math>M,N</math> be connected, complete, locally symmetric Riemannian manifolds, and let <math>M</math> be simply connected. Let their Riemann curvature tensors be <math>R,\overline{R}</math>. Let <math>x\in M,y\in N</math> and

: <math>I:T_xM\rightarrow T_yN</math>

be a linear isometry with <math>I(R(X,Y,Z))=\overline{R}(I(X),I(Y),I(Z))</math>. Then there exists a locally isometric covering map

: <math>F:M\rightarrow N</math>

with <math>F(x)=y</math> and <math>D_xF=I</math>.

'''Corollary''': Any complete locally symmetric space is of the form <math>M/\Gamma</math>, where  <math>M</math> is a symmetric space and <math>\Gamma\subset \mathrm{Isom}(M)</math> is a [[discrete subgroup]] of isometries of <math>M</math>.

== Classification of [[space form]]s==

As an application of the Cartan–Ambrose–Hicks theorem, any simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold with constant [[sectional curvature]] <math>\in\{+1, 0, -1\}</math> is respectively isometric to the [[Sphere|''n''-sphere]] <math>S^n</math>, the [[Euclidean space|''n''-Euclidean space]] <math>E^n</math>, and the [[Hyperbolic space|''n''-hyperbolic space]] <math>\mathbb H^n</math>.
